h1: The 6 Best Food Processors Under $500 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Food Processors Under $500: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six food processors under $500, compared on bowl size, motor, discs and build to match your kitchen and cooking habits.
summary: The Breville BFP810 Sous Chef 16 Cup is the best food processor under $500: the largest bowl here in brushed stainless steel. The Cuisinart DFP-14BCNY is the value pick, with a 14-cup bowl and a 720-watt motor that covers dough, dicing and shredding. The Breville BFP610 suits small households, and the Paradice 9 dices.
intro: A bigger bowl does not make a better food processor, and that is the most common mistake at this price. A 16-cup bowl sounds like a bargain until you wash and store it for two cups of salsa, because small batches spread thin across a wide blade and chop unevenly. The right size depends on how you really cook, not on the biggest number on the shelf.

We reviewed eight machines in the $200 to $500 range and ranked six on spec sheets: bowl capacity, motor, included discs, build material and cleanup. The Ninja BlendSense is a blender system rather than a true processor, so we left it out. All six come from Breville or Cuisinart, which makes motor wattage, dicing and cleanup the real differences.

products.name: Breville BFP810 Sous Chef 16 Cup Food Processor
products.verdict: The 16-cup bowl is the largest here, wrapped in brushed stainless Sous Chef build.
products.description:
The Breville BFP810 Sous Chef has a 16-cup bowl, the largest in this group, and brushed stainless steel construction from the Sous Chef line. It sells in the $200 to $500 range. For batch cooking, shredding cabbage for a crowd or making dough in volume, a big bowl removes the need to work in rounds, which saves real time.

It ranks above the Cuisinart 14-cup models because the extra capacity and metal build are the more premium combination, even though the Cuisinarts cost less to store and match it on core tasks. You pay for the room and the finish. Against the BFP610, it holds seven more cups.

Buy it if you cook for a family or meal-prep weekly. The caveat is counter and cabinet space: a 16-cup machine is a commitment, and small kitchens will resent it. Skip it if you cook for one or two.
products.idealFor: Families and meal-preppers who cook big batches.
products.skipIf: You cook for one or two and have limited storage.

products.name: Cuisinart Food Processor, 14-Cup, DFP-14BCNY, 720W
products.verdict: A 14-cup bowl and 720-watt motor handle chopping, shredding and dough for less.
products.description:
The Cuisinart DFP-14BCNY pairs a 14-cup work bowl with a 720-watt motor and covers mincing, dicing, shredding, pureeing and dough. It sells in the $200 to $500 range. A stated 720 watts matters because dough and hard vegetables need torque, and a weak motor stalls on them.

It sits behind the Breville BFP810 because the bowl is two cups smaller and the build is less premium. In exchange you get the same family of jobs at a friendlier price, which is why it earns the value title. Against the FP-130, it states its motor power and its function list.

Choose it if you want one machine for most kitchen work. The caveat is that it is still a large bowl, so very small portions process less cleanly. Skip it if you mainly prep tiny quantities.
products.idealFor: Home cooks wanting one capable all-rounder.

products.name: Breville BFP610 Sous Chef 9 Cup Food Processor
products.verdict: A 9-cup stainless Sous Chef that suits everyday cooking without hogging counter space.
products.description:
The Breville BFP610 Sous Chef has a 9-cup bowl and brushed stainless steel construction from the Sous Chef line. It sells in the $200 to $500 range. A 9-cup bowl is the sweet spot for everyday cooking, with enough room for a pot of soup base and little to wash.

It ranks below the Cuisinart DFP-14BCNY because the bowl is smaller and the listing shows fewer named functions. You gain a tidier footprint and a metal feel, and give up capacity. Against the Paradice 9, it matches the bowl size without the dicing function.

Pick it for a two to four person household. The caveat is that large doughs and shredding for a party need several rounds. Skip it if you regularly cook for large groups.
products.idealFor: Small households that still want stainless build quality.
products.skipIf: You regularly cook for large groups.

products.name: Cuisinart Pro Custom 11-Cup Food Processor, DLC-8SBCYP1
products.verdict: An 11-cup machine with dishwasher-safe parts and slicing and shredding discs included.
products.description:
The Cuisinart Pro Custom 11-Cup has an 11-cup bowl, dishwasher-safe parts and slicing and shredding discs in the box. It sells in the $200 to $500 range. The dishwasher listing is the standout, since cleanup is where food processors lose people: sharp discs are dangerous to hand wash.

It ranks under the Breville BFP610 because it offers a little more bowl but less of the premium metal finish. You get convenience instead of luxury. Against the DFP-14BCNY, it gives up two cups of bowl and does not state a motor power.

It fits busy weeknight cooks. The caveat is that the listing is thinner on motor detail than the DFP-14 models, so check the wattage before you buy. Skip it if you want a stainless premium feel.
products.skipIf: You want a stainless premium feel.

products.name: Breville BFP638 Paradice 9 Processor and Dicer
products.verdict: A 9-cup stainless processor with a dedicated dicing function.
products.description:
The Breville BFP638 Paradice 9 is a 9-cup brushed stainless processor with a dedicated dicing function. It sells in the $200 to $500 range. Even cubes for salsa or mirepoix are what standard discs struggle to produce, because a spinning blade shreds and mashes soft vegetables instead of slicing them cleanly.

It ranks below the Pro Custom because it costs more for a smaller bowl, and the value is in that single dicing feature. You trade capacity and easy cleanup for precision. Against the BFP610, it matches the bowl size and adds dicing.

Choose it if you dice often. The caveat is that if you rarely cut cubes, the dicer is a feature you pay for and ignore. Skip it if you rarely need cubed cuts.
products.idealFor: Cooks who dice onions and veg weekly.

products.name: Cuisinart FP-130 13-Cup Multifunctional Food Processor
products.verdict: A 13-cup multifunctional processor for cooks who want capacity without extras.
products.description:
The Cuisinart FP-130 offers a 13-cup bowl and multifunctional processing modes. It sells in the $200 to $500 range. A 13-cup bowl sits between the Cuisinart 11 and 14, giving room for a family batch without the full footprint of a 14.

The listing is short on specifics, which is its main weakness next to better documented rivals. It ranks last because it lacks the named motor power, dicing or discs detail that justify the other picks. You get decent capacity and a familiar brand. Against the DFP-14BCNY, it costs similar money for a smaller bowl.

It works if you want a plain 13-cup option. The caveat is that you should confirm what attachments ship with it before ordering. Skip it if you want clearly documented specs.
products.idealFor: Shoppers wanting a simple large-bowl machine.

whatMatters.detail: Bowl size is measured in cups of working capacity, and it sets how much you can process at once. Too big and small jobs spread thin on the blade; too small and big jobs need rounds. Match it to your usual batch, and check the cup figure in the product title. Most households do well with 9 to 14 cups. A compact bowl also costs less to store.

Wattage tells you how well the machine handles dense dough and hard vegetables. A 720-watt motor like the DFP-14BCNY copes with dough, while an unlisted wattage is a question mark. Look for the number in the bullets rather than a vague power claim. The Breville listings here state no wattage, so ask before relying on them for dough.

Most food processors chop and shred but turn dicing into mush. A dedicated dicing function, as on the Paradice 9, produces even cubes. Check the listing for the word dicing and an included dicing kit. Without it, expect uneven pieces that vary from paste to chunks.

Parts that fit in a dishwasher save real effort, and sharp discs are the hardest part to hand wash. Check the listing for dishwasher-safe wording, and note how many pieces you must clean after each use. The Pro Custom lists dishwasher-safe parts, which most others do not.

A large processor needs counter or cabinet space, and many get left in boxes. Compare height and base size with where it will live. A 9-cup unit like the BFP610 is easier to keep out than a 16-cup one. A machine you never take out is wasted money, so pick the size you will actually keep on the counter.

faq.q: Is a bigger food processor always better?
faq.a: No. Oversized bowls spread small amounts thin and take more storage. Match capacity to your normal batch, as the Breville BFP610 does for small households. A mid-size bowl is easier to clean, store and use for small jobs than a 16-cup one.

faq.q: What is the most common buying mistake?
faq.a: Paying for cup size you never use. Most households do well with 9 to 14 cups, and the DFP-14BCNY covers nearly every job. Buying bigger than that rarely pays off unless you cook for a crowd.

faq.q: Is the Breville worth it over the Cuisinart?
faq.a: It is if you value brushed stainless build or a dicing function. The Cuisinart DFP-14BCNY matches core tasks for less, and states its motor power. Pay for the Breville only if you will use the extra bowl or the stainless build every week.

The Cuisinart DFP-14 models list dough among their functions. Check each listing for dough mentions before relying on it, especially on the Pro Custom and FP-130. Dough needs a strong motor and a careful pulse rather than a long run.

faq.q: How should I clean the discs?
faq.a: Wash the blades carefully, away from your hands. Dishwasher-safe parts, as on the Pro Custom, help, and a soft brush protects discs from dulling. Hand wash the sharpest blades even when parts are dishwasher-safe.

faq.q: Why did you leave out the Ninja?
faq.a: The Ninja BlendSense is a 72 oz blender system, not a true food processor, so it does not match this ranking. A true processor has a wide bowl and discs, while a blender sits tall and narrow.

finalTake: Buy the Cuisinart DFP-14BCNY if one capable machine should handle most jobs, and the Breville BFP810 if you batch cook for a family and want stainless build. Take the BFP610 for a tidier footprint, the Pro Custom 11-Cup for dishwasher-safe cleanup and the Paradice 9 for dicing. Match bowl size to your normal batch, not the biggest number.
